title: Linear Motion Basics
summary: Study distance, displacement, speed, and velocity using everyday motion examples and adjustable values.
objectives: Use velocity and acceleration in a straight-line motion model
Interpret how changing time affects motion

lesson.overview: Linear motion explains how an object moves along a straight path. Students begin with familiar examples like walking to school, a taxi on a road, or a bicycle on a straight stretch.
concepts: Distance is the total path covered, while displacement is the straight-line change in position.
Velocity describes both speed and direction of motion.
Acceleration tells us how quickly velocity changes.
activities: Observe how displacement changes when initial velocity increases.
Compare motion with positive and negative acceleration.
Predict final velocity before checking the simulation output.

simulation.title: Kinematics Sandbox
simulation.description: Change the initial velocity, acceleration, and elapsed time to see how motion values respond.
simulation.formulaNote: Uses s = ut + 1/2at² and v = u + at for constant acceleration.

questions.prompt: A bicycle moves 20 m in 4 s. What is its speed?
questions.explanation: Speed is distance divided by time, so 20 / 4 = 5 m/s.

questions.prompt: If acceleration is positive, what happens to velocity over time?
options: It changes in the positive direction
questions.answer: It changes in the positive direction
questions.explanation: Acceleration measures the change in velocity each second.

title: Forces and Acceleration
summary: Explore how changing force or mass affects acceleration in Newton's second law.
objectives: Use F = ma to calculate acceleration
Compare the effect of changing mass versus changing force

lesson.overview: Newton's second law links force, mass, and acceleration. When a larger force acts on the same mass, acceleration increases. For the same force, increasing mass reduces acceleration.
concepts: Resultant force is the overall force acting on an object.
Acceleration increases with force when mass stays constant.
Acceleration decreases with mass when force stays constant.
activities: Increase force and observe the acceleration response.
Double the mass and compare the new acceleration.
Discuss examples like pushing a wheelbarrow or starting a motorcycle.

simulation.title: Force and Mass Lab
simulation.description: Adjust force and mass to see how acceleration changes.
simulation.formulaNote: Uses a = F / m and estimates velocity change with v = at over the chosen time.

questions.prompt: What happens to acceleration if force doubles and mass stays the same?
questions.explanation: From F = ma, acceleration is directly proportional to force.

questions.prompt: A 12 N force acts on a 3 kg object. What is the acceleration?
questions.explanation: Acceleration is force divided by mass, so 12 / 3 = 4 m/s².

title: Work, Energy, and Power
summary: Calculate work, kinetic energy, and power from motion and force values.
objectives: Calculate work done from force and distance
Relate kinetic energy to mass and velocity
Explain power as the rate of doing work

lesson.overview: Work, energy, and power help explain how effort changes systems. Students connect formulas to lifting loads, moving carts, and operating machines.
concepts: Work done depends on force and displacement.
Kinetic energy increases rapidly as velocity increases.
Power tells us how quickly work is done.
activities: Change force and compare the work done.
Increase velocity to see how kinetic energy changes.
Discuss which machine does more work in less time.

simulation.title: Energy Explorer
simulation.description: Adjust force, distance, mass, velocity, and time to compare work, energy, and power.
simulation.formulaNote: Uses W = Fd, KE = 1/2mv², and P = W/t.

questions.prompt: If a 10 N force moves an object 6 m, what work is done?
questions.explanation: Work equals force times distance, so 10 x 6 = 60 J.

questions.prompt: Which change increases kinetic energy the most?
questions.explanation: Kinetic energy depends on the square of velocity, so velocity changes have a strong effect.
